subject: english-language
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: A writer's TONE in "Honestly, what a complete and utter shambles this has become" is best described as:
questions.explain: The dismissive phrasing conveys scorn and frustration.

questions.q: Identifying a writer's VIEWPOINT means working out:
options: Their attitude or opinion towards the subject
questions.explain: Viewpoint is the writer's stance or attitude on the topic.

questions.q: Which is the clearest sign of the intended AUDIENCE in "Top tips for surviving your first term at uni"?
options: It is aimed at retired people
Casual language and the reference to "uni" suggest young/new students
questions.explain: Informal tone and student-focused content signal a young, new-undergraduate audience.

questions.q: Which sentence uses a fronted adverbial to vary sentence structure?
options: Without warning, the alarm shattered the silence.
The silence was shattered by the alarm.
The alarm was loud and it shattered the silence.
questions.explain: 'Without warning' is an adverbial placed at the front of the sentence for variety and effect.

questions.q: An advert claims its drink is "loved by champions everywhere." The phrase "loved by champions" is an example of:
questions.explain: A vague, flattering and unsourced claim is persuasion rather than verifiable fact.

questions.q: "This shameful, disgraceful waste of money makes me furious." The underlined choices are best described as:
questions.explain: Words chosen to stir strong feeling (shameful, disgraceful, furious) are emotive language.

questions.q: Which of these is a FACT rather than an opinion?
options: This is the best film ever made
The film is too long and dull
questions.explain: A runtime can be checked and verified, making it a fact; the others are judgements.

questions.q: "Year after year, ton after ton, our oceans drown in plastic." The repetition of "after" mainly works to:
options: Stress the relentless, ongoing scale of the problem
questions.explain: Repeating "after" emphasises a continuous, mounting build-up, stressing the scale.

questions.q: You are writing a magazine article. Which feature is most typical of the article form?
options: A signed-off complimentary close like 'Yours sincerely'
An engaging headline and a subheading that draws the reader in
A scene number and act heading
questions.explain: Articles use headlines and subheadings to grab attention and signpost content.

questions.q: "Over 90% of teachers agree that homework helps." Which persuasive device is used here?
questions.explain: A figure or percentage used to support a point is a statistic.

questions.q: "Picture yourself sinking into warm golden sand as gentle waves lap at your feet." The main method used to persuade here is:
options: Appealing imagery that helps the reader imagine the scene
questions.explain: Vivid sensory imagery invites the reader to picture and desire the experience.

questions.q: Which opening best establishes atmosphere in a piece of descriptive writing?
options: This is a description of a foggy street I once saw.
A thick fog curled through the empty streets, muffling every sound.
I will now describe a street that was foggy.
The street was foggy and quiet and empty that day.
questions.explain: Sensory, image-rich detail immediately builds mood and draws the reader into the scene.

questions.q: Which feature most clearly signals that a text's purpose is to INFORM rather than persuade?
options: Neutral, factual statements presented in a balanced way
Commands telling the reader what to do
questions.explain: A neutral, balanced presentation of facts is characteristic of writing that informs.

questions.q: When asked to identify the AUDIENCE of a text titled "A Beginner's Guide to Filing Your First Tax Return," the clearest clue is that it targets:
options: People doing this task for the first time
questions.explain: The words "beginner" and "first" signal an audience new to the task.

questions.q: For an article aimed at teenagers about social media, which register is most suitable?
options: A lively, accessible tone with some direct address
questions.explain: Matching register to a teenage audience means engaging but clear, not stuffy or patronising.

questions.q: A columnist writes: "Of course, some will say the scheme is too costly. But can we really put a price on safety?" This technique of raising and then dismissing the opposing view is:
questions.explain: Acknowledging an objection and then countering it is a counter-argument or rebuttal.

questions.q: A writer shares a short personal story about losing their dog to illustrate a point. This technique is an:
questions.explain: A brief personal story used to support an argument is an anecdote.

questions.q: Which sentence is the strongest example of using a metaphor in descriptive writing?
options: The night sky was dark, with some stars showing.
The night sky looked like it had stars in it.
The night sky was very dark and a bit cloudy.
The night sky was a black ocean drowning every star.
questions.explain: Calling the sky 'a black ocean' directly identifies it as something else, creating a vivid metaphor.

questions.q: Which sentence uses the most ambitious, precise vocabulary?
options: The big house was really old and bad.
The derelict mansion loomed, its decaying facade menacing the street.
The old house was scary and big.
The house was very very scary.
questions.explain: 'Derelict', 'loomed', 'decaying' and 'menacing' are precise, ambitious word choices.

questions.q: "Do we really want our children breathing this filthy air?" Which technique is this?
questions.explain: It is a question asked for effect, not for an answer: a rhetorical question.

questions.q: You are writing a review of a film. Which feature suits the form best?
options: A balanced judgement supported by specific examples and a recommendation
A formal salutation and address block
questions.explain: Reviews give an evaluative judgement backed by examples and end with a recommendation.

questions.q: In persuasive writing, what is the effect of using a rule of three (a triplet)?
options: It makes the writing harder to read
It creates rhythm and emphasis, making the point more memorable
It removes the need for evidence
It signals the end of the piece
questions.explain: A triplet adds rhythm and emphasis, making ideas stick in the reader's mind.
